title: Hollandaise Sauce
subtitle: classic warm butter emulsion sauce
excerpt: Hollandaise is a warm emulsion of egg yolk and clarified butter. It is rich, glossy, and slightly sharp from lemon juice. The technique is straightforward once you understand the heat -- too much and the eggs will scramble, too little and the sauce will not thicken.
sourceNotes: One of the five French mother sauces codified by Escoffier. Despite the name, its precise French or Dutch origins are debated. It became a cornerstone of French classical cuisine in the 19th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Hollandaise does not keep well. Make it just before serving and keep warm over hot water for up to 1 hour.

content.text: The bowl must not touch the simmering water below. You want gentle, indirect heat. If the bowl gets too hot, remove it immediately and keep whisking.
Put the egg yolks, vinegar, and 1 tablespoon of cold water in a heatproof bowl. Set over a pan of barely simmering water.
Whisk constantly until the mixture is thick, pale, and has doubled in volume. It should leave a visible trail when you lift the whisk.
Remove the bowl from the heat. Begin adding the warm melted butter very slowly, a few drops at a time, whisking constantly.
As the sauce thickens, you can add the butter in a thin, steady stream. Continue until all the butter is incorporated.
Whisk in the lemon juice, mustard, cayenne, and salt. Taste and adjust seasoning. Serve immediately or keep warm over hot water.

items.symptom: Sauce has split and looks oily
items.cause: Butter added too fast or heat too high
items.fix: Whisk a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl. Very slowly whisk the split sauce into it, drop by drop.

items.cause: Reduced too much or too little liquid
items.fix: Whisk in a teaspoon of warm water until the right consistency.
This batch cannot be saved. Start again with a lower heat.

content.text: Hollandaise is one of the five classical French mother sauces. It is served with asparagus, poached fish, and poached eggs. Its origins are disputed -- the name suggests a Dutch connection, but the technique is firmly French. It was codified by Escoffier in the late 19th century and remains a benchmark of classical cooking technique.
